Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01

Proposed Resolution for Joint Action to Redesign the Office of the Ombuds The Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC) December 12, 2024 Resolution The purpose of this resolution is to request immediate joint action by the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President as co-equal governing partners through the creation of a special joint committee.
The special joint committee will create a new Office of the Ombud.
Context In 2024, the Ombuds Dr.
Gerry Tyler and Dr.
Al Killilea were replaced by an Interim Ombud, Dr.
Charles Collyer.
An Interim Ombud role was created so that the Faculty Senate Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC), The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC), and the office of Provost could take a year to redesign and re-establish a new Office of the Ombuds.
This resolution grows out of discussions that have taken place between SCLC, FSEC, and the Office of the Provost.

Expectations Membership of the special joint committee shall consist of advocates for those members of the campus community who may need or want to engage with the Office of the Ombuds: representatives from the faculty and delegates representing staff and student interests. ● Special joint committee co-chairs.
The committee shall be co-chaired by a designee from the SCLC and a designee from the Office of the President.
The co-chairs shall recruit committee members and manage and oversee the work of the committee until a new Office of the Ombuds is established. ● Committee charge.
The committee shall study best practices and decide the most appropriate actions for the design and creation of an effective Office of the Ombuds, including: ● Role, duties, powers and privileges.
The committee shall revise and update the policy that delineates the expectations of the Office of the Ombud and that codifies the duties, powers, and privileges of the Ombuds.

The position requires that the Ombuds are: ● Trained in how to listen and help identify issues and courses of action, mediate conflict or disputes, and guide and direct those in need ● Skilled and certified conflict mediators ● Connected to the university community, whether currently or formerly employed by the institution

● Provided equitable compensation for their work ● Provided with appropriate space ● Provided a community infrastructure, including but not limited to a cohort of others who work in the support system of the institution (CED, EEOC, Title 9, etc.) ● Job description, nomination, application and selection process. ● Job description.
The committee will develop a new job description that must convey the following critical ideas (per section 5.88.10 of the University Manual): the Ombud role shall be to: investigate complaints from students, faculty, and administrative personnel, with the very explicit charge to handle situations that fall outside of the auspices of the usual channels (such as the Office of Community, Equity, and Diversity, the unions, office of DEI in the respective colleges, EEOC, Title IX, and Human Resources).
The Ombuds are designated to handle primarily issues that stem from interpersonal conflicts. ● Application, hiring committee, and selection process.

The committee must also design a written application (whether it be an essay on qualifications and interest, or short answers to prompts) and an application and selection process that shall include a designated hiring committee.
The hiring committee shall include representatives of the university’s co-equal governing partnership: the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President.
The hiring committee shall review applications, interview candidates, and collectively make the final decision on the selection of at least two Ombuds.
It is important that there are at least two Ombuds, especially if they are full-time tenure track faculty, or faculty and staff, from two different colleges.
This allows for recusal from cases if necessary.
The SCLC recommends a two-person Office with one faculty representative and one staff representative. ● Nominations.

The Manual (5.88.11) indicates that The Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee shall jointly nominate one or more full-time, tenured faculty or emeritus faculty for the post of Ombuds and shall submit the names of nominees to the Faculty Senate for confirmation, no later than May 1st of the year in which the Ombuds’ term is to begin.
Revisions must make certain that it is clear that nominations are not restricted to those put forth by any member of the administration and the Faculty Senate, but will follow the nomination and selection process designed and approved by

the special joint committee, which shall include the possibility of self-nominations. ● Visibility, privacy, and confidentiality. ● Physical space.
The committee must negotiate a new neutral space for the Office of the Ombuds that will achieve two critical goals: making the Office more visible to community members and also guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to enter that space to benefit from this valuable resource. ● Communication avenues.
The committee will be charged with designing communication avenues and reporting protocols that will guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Digital space.
The committee will be responsible for the redesign of the Office of the Ombuds website to improve its online visibility so that the Office functions as the first stop in the reporting line.
The website must include clear messaging that is aligned with the University Manual, a more effective and reliable submission mechanism, clear expectations regarding potential courses of action and outcomes, and any other additional information that would enhance the user experience.

It would also be helpful to link the Office of the Ombuds to the other offices that handle certain student and personnel concerns, such Title IX and the CED office’s website, to increase visibility and clarity in messaging about its services.
This includes providing clear information about what the Office of the Ombuds does (and does not do).
This information is especially pertinent for new hires and newly admitted students, as well as providing ongoing messaging directed at URI employees and students. ● Reporting and Accountability.
Record keeping and reporting are critical features of a well-functioning ombud office. ● Case Reporting and Mechanisms of Accountability.
This committee must establish a policy about reporting cases, mechanisms of accountability, report storage, etc.
The reporting must not be compromised by the bureaucratic structure and must guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Reporting and Accountability Cohort.
The committee must create an ecosystem/cohort of other staff who are working within reporting and resolution, such as the EEOC officer, Assistant Deans

focusing on DEI, the Office of Community Equity, and Diversity, Title 9 Officer, Dean of Students, representative from HR, among others. This cohort shall meet at least twice every semester. ● Consultancy. If supported financially, the committee will work with an outside consultancy to assist in the design and creation of the new office to achieve these goals.
Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-02 Faculty Senate Meeting of December 12, 2024 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS , following considerable self-study, and with significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They unite students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS , Contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences;” and WHEREAS , Honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS ,Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to a student’s interests and needs; and WHEREAS , Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED , that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously. Adopted this 12th day of December, 2024. ____________________________________________________________ Theodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

CONTRACTS: URI Catalog Information Honors Contracts Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. The following restrictions apply. (Any exceptions must be approved in advance by the Honors Program): 1. Honors contract credits shall not amount to more than one-third (1/3) of a student’s total coursework required for graduation from Honors. 2. Students shall not engage in more than one honors contract per semester. 3. Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor can they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses at other institutions. 4. Contracted courses must be taken for a letter grade and must be completed with a grade of B or better to count towards Honors Program requirements. 5. Students who do not complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor will not earn Honors credit for the course.

CONTRACTS: For the Honors Program Web site. The Honors Contract Process The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1. Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2. Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3. Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4. Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract completion form conﬁrming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work. 1: Crafting the Honors Contract The Honors Contract is a mutual commitment to a learning experience above and beyond normal course requirements. The student and instructor must agree on the criteria for evaluating the project and its scheduling. Instructors are under no obligation to supervise Honors Contracts. The Honors contract is intended to enrich the student's education by further work of mutual interest to the student and instructor, rather than simply adding to the course’s workload. Students would therefore be wise to consider projects where the enriched assignment or activity also suits the interests and needs of the instructor. An Honors contract should involve 6 to 7 hours per credit: A 3-credit course should, for example, involve approximately 20 hours of additional work. These estimated hours should include 2-3 hours of meetings with the instructor: one at the start, one mid-project, and one to conclude. Overall, plan for 3-5 hours of direct faculty involvement, including evaluation.

While the details of contracted assignments and activities may vary greatly, course enrichments could include: • Collaboration with the instructor on a joint research project. • An analytical, research, or policy paper, in addition to any assigned in the "regular" syllabus, and/or more reliant on individual work with primary or original source material. • An experiential- or service-learning experience, or internship related to the course focus. • A multimedia project, performance, or artistic work related to the course focus. • Curriculum development projects, such as assisting the professor with the development and implementation of new teaching tools, class activities, or trial runs of new course projects. [INSERT CALENDAR/ TIMELINE HERE.] 2: Submission of the Contract Proposal All Honors contract proposals must be submitted no later than the end of the third week of classes. The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1. The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2. A copy of the original course syllabus 3. A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1. What? Why? When? How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2. How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.

3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be? 4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the ﬁnal product.
The ﬁnal deadline can be no later than the scheduled ﬁnal exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.

Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.
Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed. 3: Completion of the Contracted Work Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule.
The project may, however, evolve as it progresses.
Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal.
However, the student and instructor

may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. 4: Submission of the Completed Work and Contract Completion Form To earn Honors credit for the course, students must complete the proposed work at a level deemed satisfactory by the instructor. Following that, an "Honors" designation appears on the transcript, and all credits earned for the course count towards fulﬁllment of the Honors Program, provided that the ﬁnal course grade is B or better. Work assigned by the contract is not calculated into the ﬁnal course grade. Final grades are calculated per the professor's original syllabus, reﬂecting the quality and content of all the student's coursework. As soon as the contracted work is complete and approved by the instructor, the student will submit a copy of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form no later than by the end of business on the last day of the ﬁnal examination period. If, however, a presentation or performance is part of the proposal, please invite members of the Honors Program to attend.

Amended Text For: "Honors Program" in "Special Academic Opportunities" in URI'S catalog (Added text is in red) Honors Program The University Honors Program offers motivated students opportunities to broaden and deepen their intellectual development.
The program consists of courses that emphasize discussion and project-based learning, a colloquium that brings nationally and internationally distinguished speakers to campus, and independent research projects under the guidance of a faculty sponsor.
Honors courses at the 100 and 200 levels fulﬁll general education requirements; those at the 300 and 400 levels are more specialized and often are used to fulﬁll either a general education requirement or the requirements of a major.
Students may participate in the Honors Program if they meet the following standards: Sophomores, juniors, and seniors must have earned at least a 3.40 cumulative grade point average at URI; transfer students must have received a GPA of 3.40 or better at their previous institution to be eligible for honors courses.

Incoming freshmen are invited to participate in the Honors Program based on one of the following: they must have earned a cumulative grade point average (recalculated) of 3.60 or higher in high school and must have a combined score of 1,300 on the critical reading and math portions of the SAT exam (or ACT score of 27 or higher); or they must have earned a cumulative 3.80 GPA (recalculated) in high school, and SAT scores are not considered.
Eligible students may participate in the Honors Program in one of two ways: they may take honors courses on an occasional basis, registering for any number or pattern of courses that interest them; or they may do honors work on a regular basis, meeting the speciﬁc requirements to receive the transcript notation “Completed the University Honors Program.”

No more than one third (1/3) of a student's total credits toward Honors certiﬁcation may be obtained through the use of Honors Contracts, unless an exception is granted ahead of time by the Honors Program. To achieve this certiﬁcation a student must complete a minimum of 18 honors course credits that meet the following requirements: 1) three credits in Honors at the 100 or 200 level; 2) three credits of Honors Colloquium; 3) three credits in Honors at the 300 or 400 level; 4) six credits at the 400 level, which may be either six credits of Senior Honors Project (HPR 401, 402) or three credits of Senior Honors Project (HPR 401) and three credits of Senior Honors Seminar (HPR 411/412, or other approved Senior Seminar); 5) three additional honors credits taken at any level; and 6) a 3.40 grade point average for honors courses and a 3.40 cumulative grade point average.

Honors Contracts: FAQ for Faculty For the URI Honors Program Web Page (Draft Dec. 4, 2024) What is an Honors Contract? Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. Why should we use Honors Contracts? Honors Contracts offer several beneﬁts: Flexibility: They allow students to tailor their education to their interests and goals. Accessibility: They provide opportunities for honors-level work when there are limitations on the number of honors courses offered. Student Engagement: They empower students, foster motivation, and facilitate mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. Who can supervise an Honors contract? All full-time faculty may supervise an Honors contract. No one, however, is required to do so. Part-time faculty and staff may supervise contracts only in special cases if an exception is granted prior to the creation of a contract by the Honors Program. What are the faculty roles and responsibilities in an Honors contract? Faculty roles and responsibilities include: Helping the student formulate a proposal for an appropriate contract project.

Deﬁning the terms and timeline of the contract with the student.
Providing guidance as the student works on the contracted project, with at least one mid-project meeting.
Evaluating the contract project at the end of the semester.
How much time should faculty plan to devote to this?
Generally, a faculty member should expect to devote 3-5 hours over the course of a term on a contracted project.
How are Honors Contracts set up?
The Honors Program provides comprehensive guidelines and support for setting up contracts on its Web site (See “The Contract Process”.
Students are encouraged to communicate early with instructors and the Honors Program to explore possibilities and ensure a clear understanding of the process.
Brieﬂy: The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1.
Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2.
Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3.
Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4.
Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form confirming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work.
What should be included in an Honors Contract?
The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1.

The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2.
A copy of the original course syllabus 3.
A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1.
What?
Why?
When?
How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2.
How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.
I.e: A clear articulation of how the contract meets the "broader, deeper, more complex" criteria of the National Collegiate Honors Council. 3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be?

4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the final product.
The final deadline can be no later than the scheduled final exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.
Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.

Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed.
What are some examples of positive outcomes from Honors Contracts?
When well-managed, Honors Contracts can: • Cultivate personalized learning experiences. • Develop strong mentoring relationships between students and faculty. • Enhance the overall honors experience. • Provide faculty with a new vision for their courses.
What are some potential problems with Honors Contracts, and how can they be avoided?
Some potential issues include: Routine or Casual Use: Contracts should not become commonplace or be considered a replacement of the regular honors curriculum.

Lack of Meaningful Interaction: Although the contracted projects require only about 20 hours of work by the student and 3 to 5 hours of work by the faculty, it is important to ensure that contracts involve meaningful interaction between students and instructors. Unclear Expectations: The Honors Program provides clear guidelines and assessment criteria to students and faculty maintain high standards. Faculty are be expected to provide clear instructions to the students in the contract language. How can I ensure that Honors Contracts are effective? To ensure effectiveness: Maintain high standards and clear expectations. Ensure that the contracted work is well-connected to the course themes and outcomes. Ensure that the contracted work enhances the student’s experience of the course themes, materials, and outcomes. Will I be compensated for my work with Honors Contracts? Yes, it is essential that faculty are recognized and compensated for the additional work involved in Honors Contracts. Your work should be noted in your review portfolio. What is the difference between an Honors contract and an Honors Project? An Honors contract deﬁnes a project requiring approximately 20 hours of work, appended to an existing non-Honors course to allow the course’s credits be counted as Honors credits. An Honors project is a mentored independent study for 3 or 6 credits, devoted to a project that requires extensive research, reading, writing, creativity, or experimentation.

How is an Honors contract satisﬁed? An Honors contract is satisﬁed when the professor notiﬁes the Honors Program that the student has completed the assigned task satisfactorily. The student must also receive a B or higher in the course in order to earn Honors credit. Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule. The project may, however, evolve as it progresses. Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal. However, the student and instructor may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. What happens if a student fails to complete an Honors contract? If a student fails to complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor, they will not receive Honors credit for the course. Can Honors contracts be applied to all courses? No, Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor should they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses taken at other institutions.

The MPH program would be very appealing to many students graduating from URI.
Specifically, we believe that the URI students majoring in public health, human development and family science, nursing, and nutrition will be interested in obtaining an MPH.
In addition, students enrolled in graduate programs in the College of Pharmacy and the College of Health Sciences would likely be interested in the program.
Furthermore, an MPH is often completed in tandem with graduate certificates.
The MPH could interest all residents of RI who would like to earn an MPH but would prefer to attend a state school versus a private university due to the lower program costs.
There are about 60 accredited schools of public health and more than 100 accredited public health programs.
Rhode Island is one of the few states that does not have an MPH offered by a state university.
The proposed MPH degree is a generalist (e.g., no specialization), and there are other generalist MPH degrees offered in New England.
It is important that states offer an MPH at state colleges/universities to provide affordable and accessible training that promotes health equity.

PROGRAM REPORT CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-07B At the April 2, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BS – Computer Science, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A The proposed curriculum revision modernizes the B.S. in Computer Science to reflect contemporary computing practice while maintaining academic rigor.
The revision introduces a formal specialization structure with focused pathways in Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity; and a flexible option, while streamlining major requirements to improve time-to-degree without reducing total credits or academic standards.
The specialization structure also allows for the addition of future specializations to meet the demand of this rapidly changing field.

We are proposing the following changes to major requirements: - Remove CSC 106, reducing time-to-degree by one semester. - Add CSC 310 as a core requirement, ensuring all graduates gain essential expertise in data -driven decision-making and AI/machine learning, skills that are now fundamental across all computing domains. - Remove MTH 142, acknowledging that MTH 141 provides sufficient mathematical foundation for required CS courses. - Add STA 409 to ensure consistent mathematical preparation for machine learning, data analysis, and advanced study in artificial intelligence. - Reduce the science requirement from two courses to one, allowing expanded free electives while maintaining interdisciplinary science exposure. - Refine the writing requirement course list to align with general education requirements. - Implement formal specializations in Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, and General Computer Science, replacing loosely defined electives with coherent learning pathways aligned with high -demand employment sectors.

This curriculum revision strengthens the Computer Science major through internal reallocation of Department resources rather than expansion.
The proposed changes maintain the same total credit requirements (120 credits, 56 in major) while improving student outcomes through streamlined prerequisites and providing clearer career pathways via formal specializations in the two highest-growth computing sectors: Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity.
For students, the revision delivers a contemporary curriculum that reflects current industry practice without compromising academic rigor.
For the Department, the changes ensure alignment with national curriculum standards, facilitate enrollment management through reduced bottlenecks, and enhance recruitment by offering competitive specializations in the technology industry's most in-demand areas.
The clear program structure with AI and Cybersecurity pathways strengthens program identity for accreditation, assessment, and marketing to prospective students.

For the University, the revision supports improved graduation rates, responds directly to workforce demand for specialized computing skills, and strengthens the institution's position in a highly competitive academic market.
The proposal requires no new resources, no additional faculty, and no changes to total credit hours.
It simply reorganizes existing offerings to better serve students and meet contemporary educational standards.
The Department respectfully requests approval of these curriculum changes to maintain the competitiveness and academic quality of the Computer Science program while positioning our graduates for success in the rapidly evolving fields of computing.
Specialization – Artificial Intelligence (CSC BS) Appendix B The specialization in Artificial Intelligence equips students with a progressive pathway from core machine learning concepts through advanced topics in deep learning, large language models, statistical learning, and scalable data algorithms.

Anchored by CSC 461 (Machine Learning) as a required gateway course, the specialization ensures that every student develops foundational competency in machine learning before advancing to two upper-division electives drawn from a curated menu spanning neural networks and deep learning (CSC 561), big data algorithms (CSC 546), multivariate statistical learning (STA 441), and special topics in AI (CSC 581).
We are in the process of reactivating artificial intelligence (CSC 481), which was removed from the catalog because it had not been taught recently.
We plan to add it to the rotation of courses once it is reactivated.
Additionally, we have 2 new courses in the Kuali pipeline, large language models (CSC 455) and machine learning security and privacy (CSC 465).
These courses have been taught in the last couple of years as special topics (CSC 492/592) for undergraduate and graduate students.
Until these courses are approved, students can use them to fulfill requirements with departmental permission.

Built on the program's core computer science requirements, this three -course specialization delivers the theoretical depth and applied judgment graduates need to design, evaluate, and responsibly deploy intelligent systems across diverse computing domains.
The specialization directly implements recent trends in CS education, which identify machine learning and artificial intelligence as central knowledge areas for contemporary CS graduates and implement coherent depth pathways beyond introductory ML/AI expos ure.
Critically, this specialization reflects a fundamental shift in the discipline itself: artificial intelligence is no longer a peripheral subfield, it is now core to how software systems are designed, deployed, and evaluated across virtually every application domain.
The strongest AI practitioners are not narrow specialists but professionals with deep computer science foundations in algorithms, systems, and software design, precisely what this program's core curriculum provides.

The timeliness of this specialization cannot be overstated.
AI and machine learning consistently rank among the highest-demand and highest-compensating skills in the computing workforce, and regional employers, from healthcare and defense to financial services and technology, are actively seeking graduates with exactly this preparation.
Peer institutions across New England have already established formal AI tracks or majors, and the absence of a comparable pathway at URI places the program at a direct competitive disadvantage in student recruitment.
Importantly, the Department has made investments in faculty with expertise in machine learning, data science, and AI over recent years.
This specialization now formally leverages these investments into a coherent, marketable academic pathway for undergraduate students.
Specialization – Cyber Security (CSC BS) Appendix C The Cybersecurity specialization provides students with a structured pathway from foundational security concepts to advanced defensive practice.

CSF 430 establishes core knowledge of security threats, defensive planning, and implementation of protective technologies, while CSF 432 builds hands-on competency in securing the networks and systems of real-world organizations.
Students then complete either CSF 434 or CSF 534, both of which advance into specialized topics including intrusion detection, penetration testing, incident response, malware analysis, and risk management, with CSF 534 incorporating a research dimension suited to students pursuing graduate study.
The Department of Computer Science and Statistics has developed substantial curricular expertise in cybersecurity over many years, reflected in a well-established sequence of CSF courses that, until now, have not been formally integrated into the B.S. in Computer Science.
This specialization rectifies that gap by leveraging existing departmental resources, faculty expertise, course infrastructure, and proven instructional design to offer students a coherent, named credential without requiring new courses or additional hiring.

This is particularly timely given that cybersecurity professionals are among the most critically needed in today's workforce and organizations across every sector face a widening shortage of qualified security professionals.
By formally establishing this specialization, the Department positions its graduates to meet this demand while enhancing the University's competitiveness in recruiting students who seek purposeful, career -aligned computing education.
Specialization – General Computer Science (CSC BS) Appendix D The General Computer Science specialization provides students with a structured yet flexible pathway to tailor advanced coursework to their individual interests and career goals.
Building on the program's core curriculum, students complete three additional CSC courses: one at the 300 level or above and two at the 400 level or above.
Our department currently offers many eligible courses in areas that include, but are not limited to, algorithms, artificial intelligence, computer graphics, database systems, computer systems, programming languages, and networking.

This specialization enables students to develop both depth and breadth beyond the core curriculum while aligning their studies with departmental strengths, emerging technologies, and evolving workforce demands.
Because no single specialization can encompass the full scope of modern computing, the General Computer Science pathway preserves student access to the discipline’s broad intellectual landscape.
It ensures that students whose goals lie outside established options such as Artificial Intelligence or Cybersecurity can still pursue a formally recognized course of study.
In doing so, the specialization supports preparation for diverse computing careers, interdisciplinary work, and graduate study across the field.

COLLEGE OF BUSINESS BA – Business Studies Specialization – Human Resource Leadership (BUS BA) Appendix O The proposed Human Resources Leadership specialization within the B.A. in Business Studies is designed to prepare students to lead people and organizations in a rapidly evolving workplace.
Effective leadership today requires more than technical business kn owledge; it demands an understanding of human behavior, organizational culture, social dynamics, and the systems that shape how people work together.

This specialization integrates these dimensions by combining business courses in management and leadership by using interdisciplinary coursework to deepen students’ understanding of interpersonal communication, group dynamics, diversity, equity and inclusion, and organizational systems.
Students pursuing this specialization will explore how organizations attract, develop, motivate, and retain talent, and how leaders foster environments where individuals and teams can thrive.
They will gain skills in areas such as leadership communication, conflict resolution, negotiation, and change management, while also examining the broader social and cultural factors that influence workplace relationships and organizational outcomes.
This interdisciplinary approach reflects the evolving expectations of employers, who increasingly seek graduates with the ability to manage people effectively, lead diverse teams, and navigate complex organizational challenges.
It also aligns with national trends in workforce development and talent management, where human resources leadership is emerging as a strategic driver of organizational success.

By leveraging existing courses across multiple disciplines that are not currently part of the B.A. in Business Studies curriculum, this specialization can be implemented efficiently while significantly expanding the career pathways available to graduates, including roles in human resources, talent acquisition, organizational development, employee relations, an d leadership consulting.
Specialization – Sports Management (BUS BA) Appendix P The specialization is designed to help prepare students for careers in sports management, where hands-on experiences with prospective employers and relationships are a high priority.
The specialization courses build on the leadership core to emphasize comp etencies related to entrepreneurial thinking, marketing, and sports management.
